description: Files and works the builder must never choose, with the reason. Everything here passed both gates -- right artist, right bird -- and is still wrong for this display, which is a judgement no scoring rule was going to make. `excluded` names single files; `excluded_works` names a work that is wrong for one species, which is what a series of plates needs.

excluded.reason: A study of a tawny owl's talons -- four claws on a blank page. Right artist, right bird, and nothing in the filename to say so.

excluded.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (Plate XXV) (20130813418).jpg
excluded.reason: A fine plate that the cutout beheads. The gull is standing with its white head and neck against the pale shore, the head is the same tone as the paper and joined to it, so the flood fill walks straight up the neck and takes the lot: what lands on the board is a black-backed body on pink legs with nothing above the shoulders.

excluded.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (Plate XXII) (20310404102).jpg
excluded.reason: The same beheading as the great black-backed gull, on the same shore-and-sand background, and here it takes the bill as well. What is left is a grey mantle on one leg in a lot of empty sand -- more beach than bird even before the head went.

excluded.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (Plate XXIX) (20318870755).jpg
excluded.reason: Two whole kittiwakes on a nest, and beside them a tall pale stripe the scanner caught at the edge of the facing page. It survives the cutout as its own blob, so the board would carry a vertical rule standing to the right of the birds like a doorframe.

Keulemans, from Godman's monograph of the petrels, and it is a white-faced storm petrel: white below, a dark mask through the eye, long legs and yellow-webbed feet. Ours is sooty all over with a white rump. The file is named after the volume rather than the bird, so nothing but the picture gives it away.

The second wrong petrel in a row, and a closer one: a Guadalupe storm petrel, forked-tailed and all dark where ours carries a white rump, from an island in the Pacific and extinct since about 1912. Every Keulemans petrel on Commons is a portrait of some petrel, and the search cannot tell which.

This one does contain our bird -- and a Wilson's petrel beside it, and a downy chick, and the German caption naming all three, and a ruled white border the cutout cannot get past, so the whole page arrives as a rectangle. Two species and a block of type is a page from a book, not a portrait.

Not a scan of a plate but a photograph of an open book: page edges, binding, the shadow of the gutter. The cutout has no paper to remove and keeps the whole spread, captions and all -- and the captions are two species, the Chatham Island snipe next to the godwit.

Three curlews on a rock, and the one in the middle -- the one the plate is named for and drawn around -- is a slender-billed curlew. The whimbrels are the supporting cast. A painted sky and sea behind them as well, so there is nothing to cut away either.

excluded.file: Aegithalos caudatus vinaceus & Cyanistes cyanus berezowskii 1889.jpg
excluded.reason: Five birds on one page and two of them are azure tits. The long-tailed tits are the Chinese race vinaceus, pink where ours is white, and none of the five is big enough to be the subject. The filename lists the species the way a book plate does, which is how these 1889 pages give themselves away.

excluded.file: Periparus ater rufipectus & Lophophanes dichrous dichroides & Sitta europaea amurensis & Sitta przewalskii 1889.jpg
excluded.reason: Four species named in the filename and five birds on the page: two Asian coal tits, a crested tit and two nuthatches, the Amur race and Przewalski's. The nuthatch a viewer would have to pick out is one of five small birds in a heap.

excluded.file: Poecile montanus songarus & Poecile montanus affinis & Poecile superciliosus 1889.jpg
excluded.reason: The third of the 1889 pages, and the same shape: five birds, three named taxa, two of them races of willow tit from central Asia and the third a white-browed tit. A page from a monograph, not a portrait.

Two owls side by side, and Commons says plainly what they are: barn owl on the left, ashy-faced owl on the right. The second bird is a Hispaniolan species and the larger, warmer, more eye-catching of the pair, so the board would show our owl as the smaller figure next to a bird that has never been to Britain.

excluded.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (Plate XXIII) (20132195059).jpg
excluded.reason: The gull is preening, head buried in its wing, so the one thing that says gull -- the bill and the eye -- is upside down inside the feathers. Pale grey bird on pale sand, three more birds behind it, and a wide scene at that: at 480px it is a grey shape on a yellow beach.

A landscape with a swan in it. Reeds, a far bank, a wide band of water, and the swan white on the white of the water with only its bill to say which end is the front. The board wants a bird; this is a view.

The Algerian coal tit, and the difference is the whole face: ledouci has yellow cheeks and a yellow breast where ours are white and buff. A well-drawn single bird on bare paper, which is why it scored so well, and anyone who knows the bird in their garden would say that is not it.

Captioned "1. EMBERIZA CITRINELLA MOLESSONI. 2. E. C. BREHMI." -- a type plate for two named forms, drawn to show the difference between them rather than the bird. The front figure carries a solid crimson bib that no yellowhammer on a hedge in Yorkshire has ever worn.

Two species again: Middendorff's grasshopper warbler and the Kamchatkan race of the reed bunting, three birds between them, all in the same drab brown. Nothing on the page reads as the black-hooded male anyone means by reed bunting.

What replaced the swan-in-a-landscape, and worse: the swan swims white against white water, the cutout finds no edge between them and walks up the neck, and the board gets a white shape with no head on it and the reeds still attached.

A St Kilda wren. Commons says so in the first line of the description and files it under Troglodytes; what let it through was a stray "barn owl" somewhere in the Internet Archive boilerplate the Flickr uploads carry, which was worth the twenty-two points the species gate asks for and nothing more.

excluded.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (10036178774).jpg
excluded.reason: An adult robin and a spotted juvenile in dead grass, and every colour in it -- the breast, the young bird, the grass, the fallen leaves -- lands in the same warm band. Quantised to six inks the whole plate becomes one orange-and-green scribble with a robin's face somewhere in the lower half. Fine on paper, illegible on the panel.

A cock and hen goldcrest on a mossy bough, drawn small and pale in a wide scene. Britain's smallest bird was never going to survive being fitted into a 408px box: on the board it is a knot of twigs with a yellow crown in it. Refusing this scan only fetched Commons' other copy of the same plate, so the work had to go too.

excluded.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (10560263815).jpg
excluded.reason: The right bird, the right book, and the dove is pale buff-grey on pale sand with a second bird's head beside it. There is no tonal edge anywhere for the dither to hold on to, so the panel prints a peach-coloured smear with two orange feet under it.

excluded.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (20728475732).jpg
excluded.reason: A white bird in front of dead reeds. On paper the egret is a beautiful cloud of plumes; at six inks the plumes and the reeds dither into the same speckle and the bird disappears into the bed it is standing in.

excluded_works.work: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands
excluded_works.reason: Lilford drew this gull once and Commons holds half a dozen scans of that one plate, so excluding a file only moves the builder onto the next copy of the same picture. The bird stands with its white head against pale sand, the head is paper-coloured and joined to the paper, and the cutout takes it away every time. The plate is not at fault; we simply cannot use it, and a headless gull is worse than a photograph.

excluded_works.work: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands
excluded_works.reason: The same plate, the same white head on the same pale shore, the same beheading in every scan of it. Refused as a work for the same reason as the great black-backed gull: there is nothing else in Lilford for this bird to fall back to.

A floating cask in a heavy sea with a dozen kittiwakes on and around it, sky to the top of the page. The same failure this journal gives the black-headed gull -- a seascape with birds in it rather than a bird -- and at 480px the cask reads better than any of them.

Mother Carey herself: a witch on a broomstick over a wrecking sea, with a hundred petrels the size of commas around her and rays of light coming through the cloud. A famous plate and a lovely one, and the bird in it is a motif rather than a subject. After two wrong petrel species this was the third refusal for this bird, and it is the point at which no plate is the right answer.

excluded_works.work: Nauchnye rezulʹtaty puteshestvyǐ N.M. Przhevalʹskago po t͡sentralʹnoǐ Azii
excluded_works.reason: Pleske's report on the birds Przhevalsky brought back from central Asia. Keulemans drew its plates and they are monograph pages: four or five birds of three or four taxa to a sheet, none of them British races. Commons has both the whole pages and single-bird crops of them, so refusing a file only moves the builder to the crop next door -- and the crops arrive with the neighbouring bird still clipped into the corner. The long-tailed tits in it are vinaceus, wine-pink where ours is white.

excluded_works.work: Nauchnye rezulʹtaty puteshestvyǐ N.M. Przhevalʹskago po t͡sentralʹnoǐ Azii
excluded_works.reason: The same book, and for this bird it offers rufipectus, the Tian Shan race, orange-buff below where ours is buff-white. Refused as a work because the crop and the page it was cut from are both in it.

excluded_works.work: Nauchnye rezulʹtaty puteshestvyǐ N.M. Przhevalʹskago po t͡sentralʹnoǐ Azii
excluded_works.reason: And the same again: songarus, the Songar tit, rusty-flanked and drawn with the next bird on the plate clipped in under its feet.

Keulemans drew the goldcrest once for his own book and Commons holds that plate twice, as "Regulus regulus 1869.jpg" and as "Keulemans Onze vogels 1 18.jpg", so a file exclusion just swapped one for the other. The plate is a wide bough with two very small birds on it, and small and pale is the one thing this panel cannot do.

excluded_works.work: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands
excluded_works.reason: Lilford's swan swims with two cygnets, and white on white water is the one thing this panel cannot print: the whole bird arrives as a single pale oval with an orange bill floating in the middle of it and no line anywhere to say where the swan stops and the lake starts. Onze vogels had already failed the same way, with the cutout taking the head off. Refused as a work because Commons holds several scans of the one Lilford plate.

excluded_works.work: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands
excluded_works.reason: Lilford's herring gull is the preening bird with its head inside its wing, and Commons holds scan after scan of that one plate, so excluding a file just hands over the next copy. Nothing else in Lilford shows the bird, and a headless grey shape on a yellow beach is not worth a plate.

Keulemans drew the black-headed gull for this journal three times and every one is the same gullery seen across a lake: a hundred birds forty pixels wide. Correctly identified and genuinely his, and unreadable as a portrait on a 480px panel. No plate is better than a grey landscape.
